devices.description: Casa C100G CMTS/CCAP - 13RU, 14 paired front/rear slots. Front and rear slot N are two halves of one logical position: a DOCSIS line card in front N requires its I/O partner in rear N.

gaps.note: The BDM2/BDM2m datasheet states "Total Power 300 W" in a technical specifications table headed "BDM2/2 m with 6+12 IO Card", whose RF connector row describes that card's six downstream and twelve upstream ports. The figure is the assembly's. A BDM position is TWO modules here - casa/bdm in a front bay and casa/io-6p12 in the paired rear bay, which is why casa/bdm already carries `pairs-with` - and no document we hold divides the 300 W between them. Writing it onto the front module would make the chassis total come out right and the answer to "what does a BDM front module draw" come out wrong, so neither half carries a figure and the chassis total stays a floor. The arithmetic does not settle it either way: 12 x 300 W lands on the C100G's stated 3.6 kW whether the 300 W is the pair or the front half with small rear cards. The C100G HIG corroborates the assembly reading and hedges it: Tables A-10 and A-11 both read "Approximately 300W per BDM" under titles scoping them to the BDM WITH its 6+12 I/O. THE LIBRARY IS CURRENTLY INCONSISTENT ABOUT THIS, ON PURPOSE AND VISIBLY. The three BDM variants carry NO power figure, for the reason above. The DQM and DCU cards added later DO carry one - DS8x8 220, DS8x96 320, DS8x192 350, US16x8 220, US16x4 150 - each with a `power-scope` provenance entry saying in the vendor's own words that the number covers the card WITH its I/O module and must not have a rear figure added to it. Both are defensible readings of the same problem: one keeps the per-module answer honest and the chassis total a floor, the other keeps the vendor's only published number reachable. They should not stay different once a pairing-scoped mechanism exists, and this is the record of which way each went and why, so that whoever unifies them is not guessing. THE THREE REAR RF I/O CARDS ADDED LATER FALL ON THE SAME SIDE OF THIS AS THE 6+12. casa/rfd, casa/rfu-16x8 and casa/ups-32x4 carry NO power figure, because Tables A-8 and A-9 give their port counts and connector types and no watts at all, and every figure Casa does publish for the slot is already the pair's - Table A-3 heads the DQM column "Maximum consumption with I/O module" and Table A-4 gives "Single DCU w/ RFU I/O" 200 W against "Single DCU w/ RFU UPS 32x4 I/O" 220 W for the same US16x8. Subtracting one from the other to get a rear card's share would be our arithmetic and would also be the wrong subtraction - the 20 W is the difference between two PAIRINGS, not between two I/O cards.
gaps.wanted: a pairable unit that can carry properties, so that a figure measured on a pair can be attached to the pair. The scope is now DATA - every card here declares `power-draw-scope: module-with-paired-io`, so a chassis sum knows not to add the rear partner and L30 catches it if one gains its own figure - but the scope says only THAT the figure covers a pair, not WHICH pair. The C100G HIG gives the same US16x8 200 W with the RFU I/O and 220 W with the RFU UPS 32x4, and the manifest can carry only one of them. Asking for "a per-module figure" was the wrong question: Casa states none, and one may not exist to be divided out. What is missing is the mechanism, and enough vendors doing this to design one from - Casa is the only one in the corpus.

gaps.note: The HIG body text states "Each fan assembly module has a maximum power consumption of 100W, totaling 300W across the three fan assemblies". Table A-2 of the same guide gives the row "Fan assembly (3)" as "330W maximum, 220W typical". Both are about the set of three and 300 is not 330. The contract takes 100 W because it is the only figure stated PER MODULE, which is the granularity a bay occupant needs; dividing 330 by three would be our arithmetic, not the vendor's. A chassis total is therefore 30 W light against the guide's own set figure, and no per-module typical exists at all.
gaps.wanted: a measurement from a running chassis, a vendor erratum, or a later revision of the guide that drops one of the two figures

gaps.note: Casa rates a power ENTRY module in amps and volts, never in watts. Table A-1 gives "Voltage -42 to -60VDC" and "Current 20A nominal per feed", and the chassis nameplate at Figure 1-3 gives "-48VDC, 30A per Feed (4+4 Feeds)" - but no document states a wattage, and deriving one means choosing a point the vendor left open: two current figures across a voltage range put V x I anywhere from about 810 W to 1800 W per feed. A power entry module also does not convert or regulate; it filters and distributes what the plant feeds it, so its rating is a current-carrying limit rather than the continuous output power-output-w means. The stated volts and amps are recorded in the contract's attrs; the L27 warning stays standing as the record that the watt figure is missing.
gaps.wanted: a wattage for the C100G power entry module from Casa - a nameplate photograph of the module itself would do it, or any document that rates it in watts rather than amps

a `power-draw-max-w` on each module this chassis accepts, from the vendor's own per-card table - Cisco publishes one per ambient, most vendors publish none, and until they land a module total is a floor

devices.description: Casa C40G CMTS/CCAP - 6RU, 6 paired front/rear slots. Takes the same line cards as the C100G but HORIZONTALLY, so the card is one model placed at rotate 90.

gaps.note: THE ORDERING SHEET SELLS FOUR CHASSIS AND THIS LIBRARY MODELS TWO. C40G_DS_RevA lists C40G-CHASSIS-AC and C40G-CHASSIS-DC, which are here, and C40G-CHASSIS-ACR and C40G-CHASSIS-DCR, described as "with Redundant Power and Cooling", which are not. The sheet gives the phrase and nothing else - no count, no which modules, no dimensions - and the installation guide never uses the word for a chassis variant. What the guide DOES say is that the C40G takes up to four 1100 W PSUs operating concurrently and that fewer than two cannot power a C40G-20, which tells you the supplies are redundant by population rather than by chassis. That makes the R variants most likely a populated bundle rather than different metal - but "most likely" is not a source, and inventing two configurations from a four-word description would put a guess where a part number goes.
gaps.wanted: a Casa or CommScope ordering guide saying what the R bundles contain - how many PSUs and fan modules, and whether the chassis itself differs at all

gaps.note: Casa says two things about this terminal and they do not agree. The prose in "Connecting the chassis to ground" says it "provides two M6 screws to connect a double-lug ground terminal cable". Figures 1-2 and 1-4 both DRAW three studs, in a 2x2 grid with the protective-earth mark in the fourth corner, and the two figures agree with each other. THE DRAWING IS FOLLOWED, and the model carries three. The figure is the only source that says anything about arrangement at all, so following the prose would mean inventing a layout for the two it describes; and a third stud has easy explanations - a spare, an alternate lug pitch - while a stud drawn twice that is not there has none. That is a judgement, not a reading, which is why it is filed here. THE PITCH IS NOT MEASURED FROM EITHER. It is borrowed from casa/ground-bolts@1, 15.3, off the maintainer`s hand-built C100G rear SVG. Figure 1-4 gives 13.2 across and 14.7 down for what must be one square grid - an 11 percent disagreement with itself, which is that figure`s anisotropy rather than a rectangular pattern.
gaps.wanted: a photograph of the C40G rear lower-left corner, which would settle the count and the pitch together in one look

gaps.note: The card band runs 37.5 to 386.7 in a body 432.95 wide, so it sits 37.5 from the left edge and 46.25 from the right - 8.75 mm out of centre, or 4.375 on the band's own centreline. Everything inside the band agrees with everything else; the question is whether the band is really off-centre in the metal, and nothing we hold answers it. IT IS NOT COSMETIC, and the AC input panel is where it bites. Its four C14 inlets sit behind the four front power supplies. Reflect the supply centres about the PANEL and the inlets are 1.2 out; reflect them about the CHASSIS - which is what walking round a box actually does - and they are 9.95 out. The gap between those two answers IS this asymmetry, and no arrangement of the parts inside the band can close it, because the disagreement is between the band and the chassis rather than within either. THE SUPPORTING NUMBERS ARE ALSO ODD IN THE SAME DIRECTION. The two front fan strips measure 36.0 wide each - equal, as you would expect - but leave 1.5 outside them on the left and 10.25 on the right. Two equal strips with unequal surrounds is exactly the shape of a band that has been positioned from one edge. NOT RESOLVED BY GUESSING, deliberately. Re-centring the band would move the two fan strips, the card bays on both faces, the PSU row, the PSU cover and the AC panel - and it would be one estimate reconciled against another, which this device's `pem-band-top-edge` note already records going wrong twice in opposite directions.
gaps.wanted: a dimensioned C40G front or rear elevation from Casa, or a tape measure across a real chassis from its left edge to the first card slot and from the last card slot to its right edge

gaps.note: The PEM band's BOTTOM edge at 264.5 is agreed by every source and is not in doubt. Its TOP edge is known only to about 2 mm, and the three candidates each have support: 194.0 is the direct reading of Figure 1-4 and is impossible, because the card slot above ends at 194.82; 194.82 is flush against that slot; 196.0 is what the bays carry and is what the manifest now uses, on the argument that 194.82 is an accumulation of six DERIVED slot pitches (426.6 mm over 14 slots on the C100G, carried across) and that the front face shows a measured 1.48 mm margin in the equivalent position. That argument is sound but it is an argument, not a measurement, and the whole disagreement is six pixels at 2.982 px/mm. A tape measure on a real C40G, or any Casa drawing that dimensions the rear panel, would settle it in one number. FIGURE 1-12 HAS NOW BEEN LOOKED AT AND DOES NOT SETTLE IT, recorded so nobody spends the search twice. "C40G power entry module" is the only isolated drawing of this part and the first independent look anything has had at it. Its body measures 866 x 381 px for an aspect of 2.273. The modelled 158.0 x 68.5 is 2.307 and the superseded 158.0 x 70.5 is 2.241, and 2.273 lands 0.04 percent off the midpoint of those two - at 158.0 wide it implies a height of 69.51. IT IS EQUIDISTANT AND CONFIRMS NEITHER. This guide's isolated part drawings are in any case demonstrably about 10 percent wrong about their own aspect - Figure 1-20 draws a card at 12.54 whose real aspect is 11.34 - so a 1.5 percent lean is well inside the drawing's own error. THE NUMBER IS THEREFORE NOT MOVED. It has been moved twice already, in both directions, and a third move on evidence that splits the difference would be the reconciliation loop rather than an escape from it. What Figure 1-12 does confirm is the ARRANGEMENT, which is what a figure is good for: a bolted terminal cover across the top with three fasteners, a minus pair of studs above a plus pair inside two outlined blocks, two release levers standing proud of the body top and bottom, and the yellow disconnect-power label to their right - all of which casa/c40g-pem draws. RECORDED BECAUSE THE MODULE AND THE BAY NOW AGREE, which means nothing will ever flag this again - the fit check that found the original 2 mm discrepancy is satisfied by both being wrong together as easily as by both being right.
gaps.wanted: a dimensioned C40G rear elevation, or a tape measure on the PEM opening

devices.description: Cisco ASR 9000 Series ASR 9001 Router - a 2 RU fixed-port aggregation services router with an integrated route processor, four fixed 10 GE SFP+ ports, two modular port adapter bays and 120 Gbps of fabric. Everything is on the front face: both MPA bays, both power supplies, the side-mounted fan tray and every port. The rear is a plain louvred panel.

gaps.note: The ASR 9001-S is the same metal as the ASR 9001 with two of its four fixed SFP+ ports disabled until a licence is applied. That is not a population fact - the cages are physically present and identical - so `bays:` cannot express it, and the ports are correctly drawn present in both configurations. INVESTIGATED AND IT DOES NOT REACH: `component-attrs` is the closest mechanism the format has, and it is keyed by component NAME rather than by placement id. render.py computes `comp_name = ref.split("/")[-1].split("@")[0]` and looks the overrides up by that, so `component-attrs: {sfp-ganged: ...}` would mark all SIX std/sfp-ganged instances on this chassis - both CLUSTER ports and all four SFP+ - when only two are disabled. A placement can carry `attrs:` per instance but not per configuration; `component-attrs` is per configuration but not per instance. The 9001-S needs both at once and neither mechanism spans the gap. The same edge stops this configuration carrying its own 60 Gbps fabric figure, since a configuration cannot override device attrs at all.
gaps.wanted: per-instance attrs in a configuration - `component-attrs` keyed by placement id as well as by component name would do it - or a device-attrs override in a configuration. This is a second instance of the shape recorded in docs/what-a-configuration-cannot-say.md, from a different vendor: the format can say what OCCUPIES a bay per configuration, but not what is TRUE of a part per configuration.

gaps.note: Table 4 of the fixed-port install guide gives the 10MHz and 1PPS connectors as DIN 1.0/2.3. The standards registry has no key for it - sma, smb, mcx and f-type are there, DIN 1.0/2.3 is not - so these two openings are declared as panel cutouts at their measured size rather than composed from a std/ part. Substituting sma or smb would name a connector Cisco does not. THE REASON WAS vendor-silent AND THAT WAS THE WRONG TOKEN. Cisco is not silent - it names the connector outright. What is missing is a panel-cutout dimension, which is needs-drawing, and the difference matters because the two tokens ask different things of a reader: vendor-silent reads as closed until better documents appear, needs-drawing reads as an errand somebody can run today. The correction came from asr9k-cards, who had just been wrong in exactly this direction about the XFP - concluding a figure was unsourceable after searching the intake rather than the standards - and found it in INF-8077i ten minutes after looking somewhere else. IEC 61169-8 is the somewhere else here, and nobody has opened it yet.
gaps.wanted: a std/din-1-0-2-3 part and its standards.yaml key. THE CONNECTOR IS STANDARDISED, so a sourced dimension exists to be found rather than estimated - DIN 1.0/2.3 is specified in IEC 61169-8, and any manufacturer's bulkhead-jack panel drawing carries the D-hole figure. std/mcx is the worked example of exactly this being done properly earlier tonight: registered from IEC 61169-36 / CECC 22220 at 4.95 x 4.50 with confidence verified, replacing an estimate that was 28 percent too small. This should be done the same way, and until it is, an sma or smb standing in would be a plausible wrong answer - which is the failure mode this project keeps having to dig back out

devices.description: Cisco ASR 9006 Router - the 10RU, six-slot member of the ASR 9000 Series Aggregation Services Routers. Cards mount HORIZONTALLY: slots 0 and 1 at the bottom of the cage are reserved for a redundant RSP pair, slots 2 to 5 above them take line cards. Two fan trays sit above the cage behind a hinged door, and a single power shelf below it carries the AC or DC power modules, whose inlets are on the rear face. Modelled as a BARE CAGE: every slot is a bay that a card component drops into, not a traced faceplate.

gaps.note: Cisco publishes no chassis-level power draw for any ASR 9000. Table 14's "Power Dissipation" row says only "Use the Cisco Power Calculator ... to estimate the maximum power distribution", so the chassis total is whatever its occupants sum to. Recorded in provenance as no-chassis-power-figure since the family was modelled; scoped here so a comparison can tell this apart from a figure nobody has looked for
gaps.wanted: a chassis-level maximum and typical draw from Cisco, or confirmation that the Power Calculator is the only answer the vendor will give

gaps.note: cisco/a9k-pwr-3kw-ac@1 states 142.78 mm wide. Three of them need 428.34 mm and this chassis's power shelf interior measures 416.50, so they do not fit - lint L13 flagged the overlap directly when they were placed at the measured centres. Against that, the stencil's shape box for the 'A9K Power Module' master reads 0.5477 in, which is 139.12 mm at the stencil's 1:10 scale, and my own measurement of the three openings in the ASR 9006 front master gives 138.35, 137.50 and 138.23. Those two agree to under a millimetre, and three at 139.12 come to 417.36 against a 416.50 shelf - the arithmetic a shelf that holds exactly three ought to produce. The 142.78 is most likely the art measured over something that is not the module's seating width, the same class of error as reading a card's shape box instead of its art. The bays here are sized to the measured openings, so the chassis is right and the component and the chassis disagree by about 3.7 mm until someone re-measures the master.
gaps.wanted: a re-measurement of the 'A9K Power Module' stencil master, or a Cisco dimension for the version 1 power module

gaps.note: NINE CARDS SHARE THESE SIX SLOTS AND TWO FAMILIES DISAGREE BY 32.8 mm ON THE ONE AXIS THAT HAS TO FIT ONE OPENING. The line cards and the blank filler are 395.7 mm; all four RSP-880 variants are 428.5. The measured cage opening is 352.59. The line-card story is coherent: a9k-slot-cover's own art measures a PLATE of 362.24 inside a 395.7 envelope, so the plate covers the 352.59 opening with 4.8 mm of overlap per side and the ejector brackets account for the remaining 16.7 per side. Every number has a job. The RSP-880's does not. 428.5 needs 37.96 mm of overlap per side to cover the same opening, and a card centred on this cage reaches x 22.99 to 451.49 in a 444.5 mm chassis - 6.99 mm PAST the outer wall, which is visible in the 3D view as the card's end standing proud of the side of the box. WHERE 428.5 COMES FROM, AND WHY IT IS THE SUSPECT: the RSP-880 data sheet's 'Physical specifications' row. This library's own a9k-rsp880-se provenance already records that NINE RSP AND RP MASTERS IN THE STENCIL ARE ONE DRAWING, scaled to four different stated widths - 402.8, 428.5, 428.2 and 403.4 - so "the drawing is generic across the family and cannot be all four sizes". The cage, by contrast, is measured off this chassis's own master and independently supported by Figure 19. NOT RESOLVED HERE. Two numbers describing different things is the likeliest reading - the same trap as a plate against an envelope - but nothing we hold says WHICH thing 428.5 measures, and inventing a smaller one would be the reconciliation this project keeps digging back out.
gaps.wanted: a Cisco mechanical drawing of an RSP-880 faceplate, or one measurement across a real card from ejector tip to ejector tip. Either settles it for all four variants at once and for every chassis they go in. REQUESTED FROM THE LAB, 2026-08-26, and tracked as roc-ops/Portrayal#16 - that issue carries the three conflicting Cisco figures and what to do when the number arrives.

gaps.note: NARROWED, not closed. This file and the ASR 9010's carried pitches that disagreed - 46.60 here against 44.33 there - for two chassis that take the same cards. Cisco's RSP-880 sheet resolved the 9010 half: the card is 46.0 mm thick and Cisco names the 9010 among the chassis it serves, so a 44.33 slot is impossible there and that cage is now divided on published card thicknesses. THIS CHASSIS IS NOT DISCRIMINATED BY THAT EVIDENCE. Its 279.63 mm cage admits both readings: four line card slots at 41.4 plus two RSP slots at 46.0 is 257.6, leaving 22.03 for guides; and an even six-way division at 46.60 is also >= 46.0 and so also admits the RSP-880. The even division is kept because it is what the cage measures and because nothing here favours the other, but it is an assumption and the 9010 shows the family does not always divide evenly. Neither this master nor the 9010's prints slot labels or draws cage dividers, which is why both were assumptions in the first place - the 9904, 9906, 9910, 9912 and 9922 all have a ruler in the picture and these two do not.
gaps.wanted: a dimensioned front elevation of the ASR 9006, or a per-slot width from any Cisco document

gaps.note: Two figures in b-asr9k-overview-reference-guide.pdf give the ASR 9006 body width differently. Table 13 "Cisco ASR 9000 Series Routers Physical Descriptions" (p130) says 17.50 inches (44.45 cm). Figure 9 "Cisco ASR 9006 Router Chassis Footprint Dimensions - Top Down View" (p24) dimensions the same body at 17.38 inches (44.15 cm). Same measure, same part, 3 mm apart, so this is a real conflict and not two scopes. The manifest carries 44.45 because the spec table is authoritative for overall dimensions and because Cisco's own Visio master independently records 1.9 in at 1:10 over the flanges, which back-solves to Table 13's split once the 19.05 mm flange protrusion is subtracted. The likeliest reconciliation is that 17.50 is over the outer skin and 17.38 is the sheet metal at the section plane Figure 9 cuts, but no document we hold says that, so it is not written as though one does. The height is unaffected - both sources and the stencil agree on 17.50 in there.
gaps.wanted: a Cisco mechanical drawing with a tolerance, or a tape measure on a real ASR 9006

gaps.note: The power modules load from the front but their inlets are on the rear, and the only artwork we hold for that rear panel is the stencil's ASR-9006-AC Rear master, which draws the VERSION 1 tray: three IEC inlets labelled M2, M1, M0 left to right (mirrored from the front's M0, M1, M2) with the legend "100-240V 50/60 Hz 16A MAX (3X)" and a yellow warning label. This chassis is modelled as version 2, which has four modules and therefore four inlets, and no figure in any document we hold shows the version 2 rear panel. Rather than mirror three inlets into four and invent a pitch, the rear carries the inlet panel's outer band only. The DC rear is a further unknown again - there is no ASR-9006-DC master in the stencil at all.
gaps.wanted: a figure or photograph of the version 2 AC rear panel, and of the DC rear panel

gaps.note: The air filter is real, sourced and correctly typed as a bay - Table 17 of b-asr9k-hardware-installation-guide.pdf places it along the right side accessible from the rear, and Figure 207 shows the panel and its thumb screw. What is NOT sourced is its geometry. Figure 207 is a three-quarter perspective view with no dimension lines on it, so its aspect is foreshortened and it fails gate 1 as a source of absolute size. The filter's 52 mm width and its 8 mm standoff from the rear edge are read as fractions of that figure and anchored to the chassis depth, and its height is set to the card cage band rather than measured. Treat the filter's extent as the one feature here that a tape measure would most likely move. Its presence, its side, its access direction and the fact that it is user-replaceable are all stated in words by the guide and are not in doubt.
gaps.wanted: a dimensioned side elevation of the ASR 9006, or the air filter's own spare-part drawing

gaps.note: Seven measured openings on this chassis have no occupant in the library: fan trays FT0 and FT1 (175.65 x 70.97 each), power modules M0 to M3 (103.22 x 46.34 each) and the right-side air filter (52 x 279.63). All seven are drawn as cutouts, so the sheet metal is complete and every dimension is recorded; what is absent is the parts. This is NOT the machine-findable kind of gap - a missing ref lints - but the fact that these openings are cutouts rather than bays IS invisible to any rule, and a reader could reasonably assume the chassis simply has no fan bays. It has them; they are waiting. Cisco's own numbering for them is FT0/FT1 and M0-M3 per Figure 19, and the groups are ready to be reinstated with index-origin 0.
gaps.wanted: an ASR 9006 fan tray, the version 2 AC and DC power modules, and the chassis air filter

devices.description: Cisco ASR 9010 Router - the 21RU, ten-slot member of the ASR 9000 Series Aggregation Services Routers. Cards mount VERTICALLY across the full width of the cage: the two CENTRE slots, 4 and 5, are reserved for a redundant RSP pair, with four line card slots either side of them. A cable management tray runs along the top, two stacked fan trays and a front air intake sit below the cage, and two power shelves fill the bottom. Modelled as a BARE CAGE: every slot is a bay a card component drops into, not a traced faceplate.

gaps.note: THESE BAY DIMENSIONS WERE GROWN TO MEET A COMPONENT AND ARE NOT MEASUREMENTS. Each was set by taking the size of a card the bay accepts, because a fit check reported the bay as too small. On this chassis: 403.10 on 8 bays - the 5th-generation envelope, 403.10 long 406.40 on 2 bays - a9k-rsp, 406.40 long The danger is specific and it is why they are listed rather than left to look like geometry. A fit check compares a bay to a component and NEITHER of them to the world, so it is satisfied by both being wrong together exactly as easily as by both being right. Every mismatch resolved by moving one side removes the signal without adding any truth, and once resolved nothing will flag it again. These are the entries where that happened, so the record survives the check going quiet. What IS independently grounded and is not in this list: the cage extents, measured off the stencil and confirmed on several chassis by printed slot labels or a card guide rail; the slot pitch; the 395.70 fourth-generation envelope, which is Cisco's own "includes ejector bracket/lever" figure; and the shapesheet sizes for the power modules and fan trays. The ejector arithmetic that explains why a bay legitimately exceeds its cage opening - 355.60 against 395.70, 40.10 mm - is also sourced, and it justifies the SHAPE of these numbers without justifying any particular one of them.
gaps.wanted: a dimensioned figure giving the clear opening of any ASR 9000 card cage, which would replace every reconciled figure above with a measured one

gaps.note: A THIRD LINE OF EVIDENCE ON THE ~428 mm CONTROL CARDS, derived rather than asserted, and it comes from parts that have nothing to do with the question. The vertical space available to a card is bounded by whatever structure sits above and below its cage, and on this chassis that space measures the figure recorded in card-envelope-headroom below. A card envelope larger than that cannot be installed whatever any data sheet says, because something else is already there. Applied across the family: ASR 9010 399.96 mm between the cable management tray and the card guide bar ASR 9910 421.79 mm between the tray band and the front air intake ASR 9922 420.30 mm between the tray band and the fan band ASR 9912 439.21 mm - does NOT exclude 428.5, so this chassis is silent on the question ASR 9906 unbounded above in the model, so no constraint is derivable Three of the five independently exclude a 428.2-428.5 card. That is a separate argument from the slot pitch and from the ejector arithmetic, and it agrees with both. THE 9912 DOES NOT EXCLUDE IT and is recorded as silent rather than as agreement - a constraint that fails to bite is not evidence either way, and reporting it as if it were would manufacture support. The 9010's 399.96 also sits 3.14 mm under the 403.10 fifth-generation envelope its bays now carry, which is a smaller open question of the same kind.
gaps.wanted: a figure dimensioning the clear vertical opening of any ASR 9000 card cage, which would turn all of this from derived to measured

gaps.note: THE SECOND AXIS OF THE SAME CONFLICT, and it makes the first one much harder to explain away. The RSP-880 family is published at 428.5 mm on its long axis. Two Cisco statements fix what a line card measures on that axis in this family: Table A-10 of OL-17500-09 gives the original-generation card 14 in (355.60 mm) with NO qualifier, and the 4th-generation data sheets give 15.58 in (395.70) explicitly "including ejector bracket/lever". The 40.10 mm between them is the ejectors, about 20 mm each end - which is also why a bay declared at the 395.70 envelope is legitimately longer than the cage opening it sits in. Against that, 428.50 does not reconcile. Subtract the same 40.10 of ejector and the plate would still be 33.45 mm longer than this chassis's measured cage - a cage independently confirmed to 0.65 mm by Table A-10's own 355.60. So BOTH published RSP-880 dimensions, 46.0 thick and 428.5 long, are irreconcilable with a cage that two unrelated sources agree on. That is why the bays were NOT inflated to hold it. Building five chassis around a pair of numbers that contradict the only independently confirmed dimension in the family would put the error into the geometry instead of into the record. The accepts keep the RSP-880 where Cisco names it; the bays stay at what the cage and the reconcilable envelopes allow.
gaps.wanted: the RSP-880's plate dimensions as distinct from whatever 46.0 x 428.5 measures, or a photograph of an RSP-880 beside a line card

gaps.note: Cisco's RSP-880 and RSP880-LT data sheet gives "Height: 1.81 in. (4.60 cm)", i.e. 46.0 mm, and names the ASR 9006, 9010, 9904, 9906 and 9910 as the chassis they are the system processor for. THAT WIDTH EXCEEDS THE MEASURED SLOT PITCH ON EVERY CHASSIS IN THE FAMILY: 9010 44.33 9906 43.42 9910 43.78 9912 44.06 9922 44.06 and three of those pitches are measured from PRINTED SLOT LABELS or a card guide rail with a spread of 0.11 to 0.20 mm - among the best-supported numbers in this library. A card cannot be thicker than its slot, so 1.81 in is not the seating width; it is most likely taken over the ejector levers, the same way Cisco's line card "Width" is stated as "includes ejector bracket/lever" elsewhere. The accepts lists keep the RSP-880 family where Cisco names it, because a compatibility claim is Cisco's to make. The bays are sized to what the measured opening can hold. So a reader will find a bay narrower than a component it accepts, and that is a RECORDED CONFLICT between two sources rather than an oversight - the alternative was to inflate five chassis' geometry to fit one published number that three independent pitch measurements contradict.
gaps.wanted: the RSP-880's seating width as distinct from its over-ejector width, or any Cisco statement of an ASR 9000 slot pitch

gaps.note: cisco/a9k-pwr-3kw-ac@1 states 142.78 mm wide. Three of them need 428.34 mm and this chassis's power shelf interior measures 416.50, so they do not fit - lint L13 flagged the overlap directly when they were placed at the measured centres. Against that, the stencil's shape box for the 'A9K Power Module' master reads 0.5477 in, which is 139.12 mm at the stencil's 1:10 scale, and my own measurement of the three openings in the ASR 9006 front master gives 138.35, 137.50 and 138.23. Those two agree to under a millimetre, and three at 139.12 come to 417.36 against a 416.50 shelf - the arithmetic a shelf that holds exactly three ought to produce. The 142.78 is most likely the art measured over something that is not the module's seating width, the same class of error as reading a card's shape box instead of its art. The bays here are sized to the measured openings, so the chassis is right and the component and the chassis disagree by about 3.7 mm until someone re-measures the master.
gaps.wanted: a re-measurement of the 'A9K Power Module' stencil master, or a Cisco dimension for the version 1 power module

gaps.note: The two RSP slots are 46.0 mm because that is the RSP-880's published thickness and Cisco names this chassis as one it serves - so 46.0 is a LOWER BOUND on the slot, not a measurement of it. The eight line card slots are 41.4 on the same basis. The 20.12 mm those twenty-two millimetres of card leave over is distributed as eleven equal guides, which is arithmetic rather than observation: the real chassis may well have wider guides between the cages and narrower ones within them. What IS solid is that an even ten-way division is impossible, since 44.33 is thinner than a card Cisco says seats here. Searched and not found: any per-slot width in the Ethernet Line Card Installation Guide, the Hardware Installation Guide or the Overview and Reference Guide, and the stencil master draws the cage as a single undivided rectangle.
gaps.wanted: a dimensioned front elevation, a per-slot width from any Cisco document, or a tape measure on a real ASR 9010

gaps.note: The ASR 9010's two fan trays occupy the band between the card guide bar at 566.51 mm and the front air intake grille at 673.60 mm - 107.09 mm for the pair, which is measured and solid. Where one ended and the other began was NOT measured. Scanning that band finds a dark separator at about 605.8 mm, but it does not bisect the band (39.3 mm above it, 66.9 mm below), so it was read as internal faceplate detail rather than the boundary, and an EVEN split was recorded as the right inference: the master labels both trays "ASR-9010-FAN", so they are the same part stacked twice and the same part is the same height. RESOLVED, AND THE SEPARATOR WAS THE BOUNDARY AFTER ALL. Dismissing it assumed the two trays fill the band, and they do not - two trays of 33.32 come to 66.64 of 107.09. cisco/asr-9010-fan was measured off this chassis's own front master at y 571.44 to 604.76, and that bottom edge and the separator at 605.8 agree to 1.04 mm: two measurements taken for different reasons, landing on the same line. Both trays are seated there now rather than split evenly, so the placement is measured and the inference is retired. What the band holds BELOW them - about 34 mm between the second tray and the grille starting at 675.08 - is still unnamed, and the band stays ONE cutout because a single opening with two trays in the top of it and intake beneath is what the guide's own cooling-path figure (Figure 71) draws.
gaps.wanted: a dimensioned front elevation, or the ASR-9010-FAN spare-part drawing

gaps.note: The card slots are bays and accept the line card and RSP blank. THE FAN TRAYS HAVE SINCE LEFT THIS LIST - cisco/asr-9010-fan now exists and both are seated as bays at the positions its own size provenance measured off this chassis's front master. The eight power module positions and the air filter are still NOT modelled as bays, because a bay must name a component that fits it and library/components/cisco/ carries no version 2 or 3 power module and no filter. Their openings ARE measured and are drawn as cutouts, so the metal is right and only the occupants are missing. The power shelf openings are 13.96 to 431.66 mm at y 811.74 and 873.33; the fan band is 566.51 to 673.60. Pointing them at the line card blank would lint clean and claim something false - a 41.4 x 395.7 filler plate does not cover a power module opening.
gaps.wanted: an ASR 9010 fan tray, the version 2 and 3 AC and DC power modules, and the chassis air filter

gaps.note: The cisco logo, the "ASR 9000 Series" wordmark and an "OPEN" legend are printed on the CABLE MANAGEMENT TRAY, not on chassis metal - the stencil master draws them inside that band. Per the skill, text on a part's own face is that part's silkscreen, so this chassis deliberately carries none and the tray is not modelled as a placement for want of a component. The band itself is measured (0 to 163.76 mm) and drawn as decor, so the metal is right and only the printing and the tray are absent. This is the same decision taken on the ASR 9006's fan tray door.
gaps.wanted: a cable management tray component carrying its own branding

gaps.note: THE BOTTOM IS THE ONLY FACE OF THIS CHASSIS WITH NO SOURCE, and it is not a gap in this file's research. There is no bottom view of ANY ASR 9000 chassis anywhere in the 78-document intake: every figure caption in all 65 PDFs was searched for "Bottom View", "underside" and "bottom of the chassis", and the result is zero hits. That is a fact about how Cisco documents a rack chassis rather than about this model - a face that sits on rack rails and is never serviced gets no figure. The face is SIZED correctly from Table 13, so a rack elevation and the 3D box are the right shape; what it lacks is any statement of what is on it. Nothing is invented to fill it, and no region is added naming the absence, because a check passed by annotating that you have nothing is worse than a check failed honestly. THIS HOLDS THE CHASSIS AT CAPABILITY 2. Front, rear, top, left and right all now carry sourced content; the bottom alone does not, and level 3's implementation requires content on all six. The written design asks only that six faces be "present, sized, and mutually consistent", which this file satisfies - the content requirement comes from `_has_content`, which was written for level 1. See docs/deliberately-empty-faces.md.
gaps.wanted: a bottom elevation, a photograph of the underside, or a way for a view to declare itself deliberately empty so that empty-by-verification counts where empty-by-omission does not

devices.description: Cisco ASR 9904 Router - the smallest modular chassis of the ASR 9900 generation, four slots in 6 RU. Cards mount HORIZONTALLY and the redundant RSP pair sits in the MIDDLE, slots 1 and 2, with a line card above and below it. A single fan tray is fitted from the rear and a power shelf of four modules fills the bottom. Modelled as a BARE CAGE. The card openings are cutouts rather than bays for now - see gaps.

gaps.note: Cisco publishes no chassis-level power draw for any ASR 9000. Table 14's "Power Dissipation" row says only "Use the Cisco Power Calculator ... to estimate the maximum power distribution", so the chassis total is whatever its occupants sum to. Recorded in provenance as no-chassis-power-figure since the family was modelled; scoped here so a comparison can tell this apart from a figure nobody has looked for
gaps.wanted: a chassis-level maximum and typical draw from Cisco, or confirmation that the Power Calculator is the only answer the vendor will give

gaps.note: The power shelf is drawn as one opening, 423.85 x 48 mm, rather than four module openings. Figure 20 and Table 15 both establish that there are FOUR modules and that Cisco numbers them M0 to M3, so the count and the numbering are not in doubt - what is missing is where the boundaries fall. The stencil master draws this shelf POPULATED, with each module rendered as a pair of fan wheels, so scanning the band returns grille detail rather than separators and the per-module pitch could not be recovered the way the ASR 9006's was from its bare shelf. An even four-way division would be arithmetic rather than measurement, and the 9006 showed the gaps between modules are not uniform with the end margins.
gaps.wanted: a bare-shelf figure, or a front elevation with the power shelf dimensioned

gaps.note: top, bottom and left are sized from Table 13 and Figure 10 (the 9904's top-down footprint) and are deliberately EMPTY. No document we hold shows any of the three. devices.description: Cisco ASR 9906 Router - the 14 RU, six-slot member of the ASR 9900 generation. Cards mount VERTICALLY and the redundant RSP pair takes the OUTER slots, 0 and 5, with four line cards between them. The layout is unusual for the family: a vertical power shelf runs down the LEFT of the card cage and two fan trays sit behind a door on the RIGHT, with a full-width air intake along the bottom. Modelled as a BARE CAGE; the card openings are cutouts rather than bays - see gaps.

gaps.note: Cisco publishes no chassis-level power draw for any ASR 9000. Table 14's "Power Dissipation" row says only "Use the Cisco Power Calculator ... to estimate the maximum power distribution", so the chassis total is whatever its occupants sum to. Recorded in provenance as no-chassis-power-figure since the family was modelled; scoped here so a comparison can tell this apart from a figure nobody has looked for
gaps.wanted: a chassis-level maximum and typical draw from Cisco, or confirmation that the Power Calculator is the only answer the vendor will give

gaps.note: THESE BAY DIMENSIONS WERE GROWN TO MEET A COMPONENT AND ARE NOT MEASUREMENTS. Each was set by taking the size of a card the bay accepts, because a fit check reported the bay as too small. On this chassis: 42.67 on 6 bays - a9k-4hg-flex, 42.67 thick 403.40 on 6 bays - a99-rsp-se, 403.40 long The danger is specific and it is why they are listed rather than left to look like geometry. A fit check compares a bay to a component and NEITHER of them to the world, so it is satisfied by both being wrong together exactly as easily as by both being right. Every mismatch resolved by moving one side removes the signal without adding any truth, and once resolved nothing will flag it again. These are the entries where that happened, so the record survives the check going quiet. What IS independently grounded and is not in this list: the cage extents, measured off the stencil and confirmed on several chassis by printed slot labels or a card guide rail; the slot pitch; the 395.70 fourth-generation envelope, which is Cisco's own "includes ejector bracket/lever" figure; and the shapesheet sizes for the power modules and fan trays. The ejector arithmetic that explains why a bay legitimately exceeds its cage opening - 355.60 against 395.70, 40.10 mm - is also sourced, and it justifies the SHAPE of these numbers without justifying any particular one of them.
gaps.wanted: a dimensioned figure giving the clear opening of any ASR 9000 card cage, which would replace every reconciled figure above with a measured one

gaps.note: THE SECOND AXIS OF THE SAME CONFLICT, and it makes the first one much harder to explain away. The RSP-880 family is published at 428.5 mm on its long axis. Two Cisco statements fix what a line card measures on that axis in this family: Table A-10 of OL-17500-09 gives the original-generation card 14 in (355.60 mm) with NO qualifier, and the 4th-generation data sheets give 15.58 in (395.70) explicitly "including ejector bracket/lever". The 40.10 mm between them is the ejectors, about 20 mm each end - which is also why a bay declared at the 395.70 envelope is legitimately longer than the cage opening it sits in. Against that, 428.50 does not reconcile. Subtract the same 40.10 of ejector and the plate would still be 33.45 mm longer than this chassis's measured cage - a cage independently confirmed to 0.65 mm by Table A-10's own 355.60. So BOTH published RSP-880 dimensions, 46.0 thick and 428.5 long, are irreconcilable with a cage that two unrelated sources agree on. That is why the bays were NOT inflated to hold it. Building five chassis around a pair of numbers that contradict the only independently confirmed dimension in the family would put the error into the geometry instead of into the record. The accepts keep the RSP-880 where Cisco names it; the bays stay at what the cage and the reconcilable envelopes allow.
gaps.wanted: the RSP-880's plate dimensions as distinct from whatever 46.0 x 428.5 measures, or a photograph of an RSP-880 beside a line card

gaps.note: Cisco's RSP-880 and RSP880-LT data sheet gives "Height: 1.81 in. (4.60 cm)", i.e. 46.0 mm, and names the ASR 9006, 9010, 9904, 9906 and 9910 as the chassis they are the system processor for. THAT WIDTH EXCEEDS THE MEASURED SLOT PITCH ON EVERY CHASSIS IN THE FAMILY: 9010 44.33 9906 43.42 9910 43.78 9912 44.06 9922 44.06 and three of those pitches are measured from PRINTED SLOT LABELS or a card guide rail with a spread of 0.11 to 0.20 mm - among the best-supported numbers in this library. A card cannot be thicker than its slot, so 1.81 in is not the seating width; it is most likely taken over the ejector levers, the same way Cisco's line card "Width" is stated as "includes ejector bracket/lever" elsewhere. The accepts lists keep the RSP-880 family where Cisco names it, because a compatibility claim is Cisco's to make. The bays are sized to what the measured opening can hold. So a reader will find a bay narrower than a component it accepts, and that is a RECORDED CONFLICT between two sources rather than an oversight - the alternative was to inflate five chassis' geometry to fit one published number that three independent pitch measurements contradict.
gaps.wanted: the RSP-880's seating width as distinct from its over-ejector width, or any Cisco statement of an ASR 9000 slot pitch

gaps.note: The vertical power shelf is drawn as one opening rather than three module openings. Figure 21 and Table 15 both establish three modules stacked M0 at the bottom to M2 at the top, so the count and numbering are not in doubt; the boundaries are. The master draws this column POPULATED - each module rendered with its own fan wheel - so a scan returns grille detail rather than separators, the same obstacle the ASR 9904's horizontal shelf presents. The column's outer rectangle is measured and drawn.
gaps.wanted: a figure showing the power shelf empty, or a dimensioned front elevation

gaps.note: The ASR 9906's rear carries the fabric card cage and we know a great deal ABOUT it and almost nothing about its geometry. There is no ASR-9906 Rear master in Cisco's stencil, and Figure 21 shows only the front. The count is sourced but indirectly: Table 13 quotes the configured weight for a chassis "Configured with two fan trays, two RSPs, five fabric cards, and one PEM", so five, and the sibling ASR 9910's Figure 22 shows fabric slots numbered from 0. Nothing states their width, their height, or where the PEM sits. The rear is therefore sized and carries regions naming what is there, with no cutouts invented to fill it.
gaps.wanted: an ASR 9906 rear elevation, or a rear photograph

gaps.note: THE BOTTOM IS THE ONLY FACE OF THIS CHASSIS WITH NO SOURCE, and it is not a gap in this file's research. There is no bottom view of ANY ASR 9000 chassis anywhere in the 78-document intake: every figure caption in all 65 PDFs was searched for "Bottom View", "underside" and "bottom of the chassis", and the result is zero hits. That is a fact about how Cisco documents a rack chassis rather than about this model - a face that sits on rack rails and is never serviced gets no figure. The face is SIZED correctly from Table 13, so a rack elevation and the 3D box are the right shape; what it lacks is any statement of what is on it. Nothing is invented to fill it, and no region is added naming the absence, because a check passed by annotating that you have nothing is worse than a check failed honestly. THIS NO LONGER HOLDS THE CHASSIS BACK, and the reason is worth recording rather than deleting. The face now carries what IS sourced about it - the two rack mounting surfaces, at 5.00 in and 9.45 in from the front - so it is no longer content-free and the chassis reads at capability 4. That is not the gap closing. The bottom still has no elevation and nothing is drawn of what sits between those rails; what changed is that the little which is published got written down. The sibling ASR 9910, which has no bottom view at all, is the one still held at capability 2.
gaps.wanted: a bottom elevation or a photograph of the underside. What is on this face between the rack rails remains unstated by every document in the intake

These are two scopes rather than two answers: the same card draws less in this chassis than in the 9922. A chassis total built from the component here is therefore CONSERVATIVE - it over-counts each of the seven fabric cards - which is the safe direction but is not the right number. The component cannot carry both without a chassis-scoped mechanism, which the library does not have; casa/c100g records the same species of problem for paired modules.
gaps.wanted: a per-chassis power scope on a component contract, or a separate PID for the 9912 variant

gaps.note: Three power shelves are drawn as single openings rather than four module openings each. Figure 23 numbers them M0 to M3 per shelf and Table 15 gives "Version 2 power system: Up to twelve AC power modules per system, four per tray" - so twelve, and the count is not in doubt. The boundaries are: the master draws all three shelves populated, so scanning returns module detail rather than separators. The shelves' vertical extents here are estimated from the band below the RP/FC cage rather than measured off separator rules, which is weaker than everything else in this file and is why they are cutouts and not bays.
gaps.wanted: a figure showing the power shelves empty, or a dimensioned front elevation

gaps.note: THE BOTTOM IS THE ONLY FACE OF THIS CHASSIS WITH NO SOURCE, and it is not a gap in this file's research. There is no bottom view of ANY ASR 9000 chassis anywhere in the 78-document intake: every figure caption in all 65 PDFs was searched for "Bottom View", "underside" and "bottom of the chassis", and the result is zero hits. That is a fact about how Cisco documents a rack chassis rather than about this model - a face that sits on rack rails and is never serviced gets no figure. The face is SIZED correctly from Table 13, so a rack elevation and the 3D box are the right shape; what it lacks is any statement of what is on it. Nothing is invented to fill it, and no region is added naming the absence, because a check passed by annotating that you have nothing is worse than a check failed honestly. THIS HOLDS THE CHASSIS AT CAPABILITY 2. Front, rear, top, left and right all now carry sourced content; the bottom alone does not, and level 3's implementation requires content on all six. The written design asks only that six faces be "present, sized, and mutually consistent", which this file satisfies - the content requirement comes from `_has_content`, which was written for level 1. See docs/deliberately-empty-faces.md.

devices.description: Cisco ASR 9922 Router - 44 RU and the largest of the family. TWENTY vertical line card slots in two cages, one above and one below a central cage of two route processors flanking seven fabric cards, with four fan trays between the cages and four power shelves across the top. The line cards in the LOWER cage, slots 10 to 19, are installed UPSIDE DOWN. Modelled as a bare cage.

gaps.note: Cisco publishes no chassis-level power draw for any ASR 9000. Table 14's "Power Dissipation" row says only "Use the Cisco Power Calculator ... to estimate the maximum power distribution", so the chassis total is whatever its occupants sum to. Recorded in provenance as no-chassis-power-figure since the family was modelled; scoped here so a comparison can tell this apart from a figure nobody has looked for
gaps.wanted: a chassis-level maximum and typical draw from Cisco, or confirmation that the Power Calculator is the only answer the vendor will give

gaps.note: THESE BAY DIMENSIONS WERE GROWN TO MEET A COMPONENT AND ARE NOT MEASUREMENTS. Each was set by taking the size of a card the bay accepts, because a fit check reported the bay as too small. On this chassis: 42.67 on 20 bays - a9k-4hg-flex, 42.67 thick 403.10 on 20 bays - the 5th-generation envelope, 403.10 long The danger is specific and it is why they are listed rather than left to look like geometry. A fit check compares a bay to a component and NEITHER of them to the world, so it is satisfied by both being wrong together exactly as easily as by both being right. Every mismatch resolved by moving one side removes the signal without adding any truth, and once resolved nothing will flag it again. These are the entries where that happened, so the record survives the check going quiet. What IS independently grounded and is not in this list: the cage extents, measured off the stencil and confirmed on several chassis by printed slot labels or a card guide rail; the slot pitch; the 395.70 fourth-generation envelope, which is Cisco's own "includes ejector bracket/lever" figure; and the shapesheet sizes for the power modules and fan trays. The ejector arithmetic that explains why a bay legitimately exceeds its cage opening - 355.60 against 395.70, 40.10 mm - is also sourced, and it justifies the SHAPE of these numbers without justifying any particular one of them.
gaps.wanted: a dimensioned figure giving the clear opening of any ASR 9000 card cage, which would replace every reconciled figure above with a measured one

gaps.note: A THIRD LINE OF EVIDENCE ON THE ~428 mm CONTROL CARDS, derived rather than asserted, and it comes from parts that have nothing to do with the question. The vertical space available to a card is bounded by whatever structure sits above and below its cage, and on this chassis that space measures the figure recorded in card-envelope-headroom below. A card envelope larger than that cannot be installed whatever any data sheet says, because something else is already there. Applied across the family: ASR 9010 399.96 mm between the cable management tray and the card guide bar ASR 9910 421.79 mm between the tray band and the front air intake ASR 9922 420.30 mm between the tray band and the fan band ASR 9912 439.21 mm - does NOT exclude 428.5, so this chassis is silent on the question ASR 9906 unbounded above in the model, so no constraint is derivable Three of the five independently exclude a 428.2-428.5 card. That is a separate argument from the slot pitch and from the ejector arithmetic, and it agrees with both. THE 9912 DOES NOT EXCLUDE IT and is recorded as silent rather than as agreement - a constraint that fails to bite is not evidence either way, and reporting it as if it were would manufacture support. The 9010's 399.96 also sits 3.14 mm under the 403.10 fifth-generation envelope its bays now carry, which is a smaller open question of the same kind.
gaps.wanted: a figure dimensioning the clear vertical opening of any ASR 9000 card cage, which would turn all of this from derived to measured

gaps.note: THE SECOND AXIS OF THE SAME CONFLICT, and it makes the first one much harder to explain away. The RSP-880 family is published at 428.5 mm on its long axis. Two Cisco statements fix what a line card measures on that axis in this family: Table A-10 of OL-17500-09 gives the original-generation card 14 in (355.60 mm) with NO qualifier, and the 4th-generation data sheets give 15.58 in (395.70) explicitly "including ejector bracket/lever". The 40.10 mm between them is the ejectors, about 20 mm each end - which is also why a bay declared at the 395.70 envelope is legitimately longer than the cage opening it sits in. Against that, 428.50 does not reconcile. Subtract the same 40.10 of ejector and the plate would still be 33.45 mm longer than this chassis's measured cage - a cage independently confirmed to 0.65 mm by Table A-10's own 355.60. So BOTH published RSP-880 dimensions, 46.0 thick and 428.5 long, are irreconcilable with a cage that two unrelated sources agree on. That is why the bays were NOT inflated to hold it. Building five chassis around a pair of numbers that contradict the only independently confirmed dimension in the family would put the error into the geometry instead of into the record. The accepts keep the RSP-880 where Cisco names it; the bays stay at what the cage and the reconcilable envelopes allow.
gaps.wanted: the RSP-880's plate dimensions as distinct from whatever 46.0 x 428.5 measures, or a photograph of an RSP-880 beside a line card

gaps.note: Cisco's RSP-880 and RSP880-LT data sheet gives "Height: 1.81 in. (4.60 cm)", i.e. 46.0 mm, and names the ASR 9006, 9010, 9904, 9906 and 9910 as the chassis they are the system processor for. THAT WIDTH EXCEEDS THE MEASURED SLOT PITCH ON EVERY CHASSIS IN THE FAMILY: 9010 44.33 9906 43.42 9910 43.78 9912 44.06 9922 44.06 and three of those pitches are measured from PRINTED SLOT LABELS or a card guide rail with a spread of 0.11 to 0.20 mm - among the best-supported numbers in this library. A card cannot be thicker than its slot, so 1.81 in is not the seating width; it is most likely taken over the ejector levers, the same way Cisco's line card "Width" is stated as "includes ejector bracket/lever" elsewhere. The accepts lists keep the RSP-880 family where Cisco names it, because a compatibility claim is Cisco's to make. The bays are sized to what the measured opening can hold. So a reader will find a bay narrower than a component it accepts, and that is a RECORDED CONFLICT between two sources rather than an oversight - the alternative was to inflate five chassis' geometry to fit one published number that three independent pitch measurements contradict.
gaps.wanted: the RSP-880's seating width as distinct from its over-ejector width, or any Cisco statement of an ASR 9000 slot pitch

gaps.note: The guide states that "line cards must be installed upside down in slots 10 through 19 of the bottom card cage, whereas in slots 0 though 9 of the top card cage, the line cards are installed right side up". This is a real property of the chassis and the model cannot currently express it. The bays for 10 to 19 are geometrically identical to 0 to 9 and carry no rotation, because the card is inverted about its own long axis rather than rotated in the plane of the panel - a `rotate: 180` would spin the faceplate end for end, which is a different thing and would put the ejectors at the wrong ends. So a card rendered in slot 15 will show its ports and its part number the same way up as one in slot 5, and on real hardware it would not. Anyone reading port positions off the lower cage should know that.
gaps.wanted: a mirror or flip transform on a bay, distinct from rotation, or a photograph settling exactly which way an inverted card reads

gaps.note: RP0 and RP1 are CUTOUTS rather than bays. The candidate component is cisco/asr-9922-rp-se/-tr, named for this chassis and carrying Table 23's "RP Card" figure of 259 W, but it declares a slot envelope of 46.0 mm and this cage's nine positions divide its measured 429.04 mm span into 47.67 mm each - which the RP would fit - while the LINE CARD cages divide into 43.388 and the rail pitch is 44.06. A 46.0 mm supervisor does not fit a 44 mm slot, and the same 46.0 x 428.5 x 628.9 appears on a9k-rsp880-se/-tr, byte for byte, which suggests one derivation reused rather than two measurements. Until that width is re-derived from the shapesheet these two positions stay openings. The seven fabric positions beside them ARE bays, because a99-sfc3's 41.4 fits comfortably.
gaps.wanted: a re-derivation of asr-9922-rp's width from the stencil shapesheet, both axes from one source

gaps.note: The four fan trays are BAYS now, seating cisco/asr-9922-fan-v3, which is how the ASR 9910 and ASR 9010 already model theirs - a fan tray is a module you pull, not a hole in a plate. That moved the complaint from L39, which could only say the opening had nothing in it, to L33, which says the thing that goes in it is 36.95 mm too wide. Same disagreement, stated where the numbers are. cisco/asr-9922-fan-v3 declares 475.96 mm wide and this chassis's BODY is 447.0, so the component is 29 mm wider than the box it goes in. Compare cisco/asr-9910-fan at 445.2, which sits inside its own 447 mm body correctly. Both are class cooling and one of them is measured against the rack face rather than the body - the stencil records rack-face widths for trays and covers, and 475.96 is within a few millimetres of the 482.6 mm rack face. The openings here are the measured bands and the component is not placed.
gaps.wanted: asr-9922-fan-v3's width re-derived against the body, or confirmation that the fan tray really does span the rack face and needs a negative offset like a mounting ear

devices.description: 2U two-socket rack server - 24 x 2.5 inch front drive bays

gaps.note: dell/riser-divider-plate-14g@1's OUTLINE AND DEPTH ARE MEASURED and its FACE IS NOT. Both bodies come off Dell's service model to the hundredth - face 267.32..278.64 and 297.10..308.42, y 1.81..42.42, 17.61 proud - but what is printed or punched on them has not been established from any figure. Riser 1's equivalent plate carries a five-slot column that appears in no cut of the model at any plane and had to be read off ISM figure 8; whether these two carry the same column, or anything else, was NOT SEARCHED FOR rather than looked for and found absent. The recess drawn for the card clip is drawn because a clip sits in a recess on riser 1, not because this plate was seen to have one.
gaps.wanted: a rear photograph or ISM figure at usable resolution across face 267..309, which would settle both plates at once - they are the same pressing

gaps.note: WHICH OF THE TWO IS IN FRONT IS ASSERTED, NOT MEASURED. dell/riser-1-top- shelf-14g@1 is 14.68 proud (measured, the chassis shell's front) and dell/riser-1-shroud-14g@1's plate is extruded at 17.76 (an approximation across a whole outline, as that file's depth key says), so the plate drew in front and the shelf read as tucked under the piece it closes the top of. The operator, looking at the render against the hardware, says the shelf is the outermost thing there. It is expressed as a 3.10 `lift` on the composition - the smallest value that clears 17.76 - so both measured depths survive untouched and only the ordering changes. If the plate's width and depth are ever settled properly (see riser-1-shroud-rib-width-unresolved, which is the same piece of missing evidence) this lift should be re-derived rather than kept.
gaps.wanted: a mechanical drawing or a caliper on the hardware giving the riser-1 shroud plate's front and the chassis top shelf's front at the same face x, which is the one measurement that settles the ordering outright

gaps.note: THE MID BAYS ARE NOT NUMBERED HERE, AND THAT IS DELIBERATE. This device numbers its front drives 0 to 23 and its rear drives 12 to 15 or 24 to 27, in both cases because Dell's own label says so and the numbering was checked against it. NOTHING FOUND SO FAR SAYS WHAT DELL CALLS THE FOUR MID-BAY DRIVES. They are `mid-lff-0..3` and `mid-sff-0..3`, which are positions and not claims: they say "the four slots, left to right" and assert nothing about what the machine prints or what iDRAC reports. Inventing a range that looked like the others - 24 to 27 say - would have been the easy thing and would have been a fabrication of exactly the kind the front and rear numbering was careful to avoid.
gaps.wanted: the mid-drive-tray page of the R740xd installation and service manual, or a photograph of the tray with its silkscreen legible

gaps.note: THE PREVIOUS FORM OF THIS GAP SAID THE CAD POSE WAS EXPLODED. IT IS NOT, AND THE SENTENCE IS KEPT HERE BECAUSE IT IS THE INSTRUCTIVE PART. A reading of R740XD_GPU_Brackets_01-1 was rejected on the grounds that its y extent ran -40 to +24 against an 86.8 mm panel - "not a seated pose". That was a Y-CONVENTION ARTEFACT IN THE READER, not a fact about the model. Calibrated against the rear handle, whose device y is trusted, the convention is face_y = 86.8 - raw_y; it reproduces the handle's low edge at 42.35 to the hundredth and this assembly's own sibling R740XD_Expansioncard_Clip-1.001 at y 1.81..44.81, the figure riser-1-shroud-14g already carried from an independent read. The pose is seated and the 36.9 mm was real all along - a plausibility check that fires on the reader instead of the data rejects good evidence, and it cost a wrong fix at the other end of the part. WHAT THE MODEL ACTUALLY SHOWS, descended to mesh children, is two levels: Body_2_3.002 at 111.70..148.60, 11.06 proud - a wide lower shelf, now drawn - and Body_1_3.005 at 125.00..135.10, 17.71 proud - a narrow rib. WHAT IS STILL OPEN is the rib. riser-1-shroud-14g draws it 120.64..137.26, about 4 mm wider on each side than the body at that depth. The outline came from cad-outline.py cutting at the panel plane, which returns the SILHOUETTE of everything the plane crosses rather than one body, so it cannot settle a single body's width. Re-cutting it would move the slot column and the clip recess, both photo-measured off ISM figure 8 and both currently agreeing with the render, so it is recorded rather than guessed.
gaps.wanted: a mechanical drawing of the riser-1 shroud, or a clean section of R740XD_GPU_Brackets_01-1 above the shelf, to settle the raised rib's width independently of the panel-plane silhouette

gaps.note: THE NUMBER CAME FROM A DESCRIPTION, NOT A MEASUREMENT. std/vga@1 stands 6.73 proud because that is what a D-sub does when its flange bolts through sheet metal, and on this machine's front the connector is on the control panel board, which sits back from the bezel - so only a little of it emerges. The operator, looking at the hardware, put that at "a millimetre and a half"; `inset: 5.23` is 6.73 less 1.50 and is therefore an estimate dressed as two decimal places. IT IS THE SETBACK THAT IS UNKNOWN, not the connector. The 6.73 is TE 114-40010's mating dimension and stays; what nobody here has measured is how far behind the faceplate the board sits. A caliper on the hardware, or any drawing that dimensions the control panel board against the front bezel, replaces one number and nothing else. THE REAR D-SUBS ARE NOT AFFECTED. They bolt through the rear panel in the ordinary way and carry no inset.
gaps.wanted: the control panel board's setback from the front bezel, measured

gaps.note: TWO NUMBERS, ONE APPEARANCE EACH, AND NEITHER CORROBORATED. This device seats both supplies at y 46.20, and the only other place that number appears is a comment on riser 2's plate saying the plate was cut back to "face 46.20 - the power supply's top edge", which cites this seating rather than a source. psu-1100w-ac-14g's provenance used to argue the module top was y 45.0, read off R740 ISM figure 9 - but it argued that in the same breath as a height of 41.8, and the height has since been measured off Dell's own service model at 39.1. A position argued from a reading whose companion number is disproven is not evidence for the position. THE CAD CANNOT ANSWER IT. glb-parts.py states the rule it enforces: sizes survive a pose and positions do not, and this scene draws the supply with its withdrawal handle swung open for a removal procedure. The body measures cleanly at 86.3 x 39.1 x 195.5 and its face y lands nowhere near either candidate. AN ATTEMPT TO RE-READ FIGURE 9 FAILED GATE 1 AT 13.18%, against a provenance that claims 0.26% for the same figure - so the failure is in the panel detection, not in the figure, and nothing may be taken off it until somebody finds the body's true top and bottom edges in that raster. The seating is left where it is rather than moved on a measurement that did not pass its own gate. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: the body edges in ISM figure 9 identified by hand rather than by ink-density, which turns the 13.18% back into the 0.26% the figure is capable of and makes the fraction readable. 1.2 mm is worth one careful pass, because riser 2's plate is cut to this number.
gaps.wanted: the supply's top edge on the rear face, from a figure that has passed Gate 1

gaps.note: Dell's model carries riser 1 (three-slot, measured here to the tenth) and the low-profile riser 2C. It carries no full-height riser 2 and no riser 3. Their bodies - the PCB and the slot connectors in `body.boxes` on dell/riser-2a/2d/2e/2f-14g and dell/riser-3a/3b-14g - are riser 1's, stood at their own bays' outer edges, and riser 3's PCB is cut to end at the supply cage it stands on.
gaps.wanted: A model or a photograph of riser 2A and riser 3 seated, which would put both PCBs where they are.

gaps.note: ISM figures 17 and 18 number five fronts - 24, 16 and 8 x 2.5 inch at bays 0-23, 0-15 and 0-7, and 12 and 8 x 3.5 inch at 0-11 and 0-7. TWO OF THE FIVE ARE NOW DRAWN. `front` is the 24 x 2.5 inch; `front-lff-12` is the 12 x 3.5 inch, the one that mattered, because it is the front the rears numbered 12-15 and 12-13 belong to. It is a variant view with `face: front`, bound by the `lff12-` configurations, and its grid was measured off dellr740xd-12x35.webp at Gate 1 0.07% - the same backplane opening the 24 SFF bays divide, 428.832 / 4 = 107.208 against a measured period of 107.216. THE 16 AND 8 x 2.5 INCH AND THE 8 x 3.5 INCH ARE STILL NOT MODELLED, and no figure for them has been measured.
gaps.wanted: the remaining three fronts as further `face: front` variants, each with a configuration to bind it.

gaps.note: DELL ENUMERATES THEM. ISM table 28, "Supported backplane options for PowerEdge R740XD systems", lists front, mid and rear together - ten rows, and the coupling falls straight out: 2.5in x24 no rear 2.5in x24 + 2.5in x4 mid + 2.5in x4 rear 2.5in x24 (20 SAS/SATA + 4 NVMe) no rear 3.5in x12 no rear 3.5in x12 + 3.5in x4 mid + 3.5in x2 rear 3.5in x12 + 3.5in x4 mid + 2.5in x4 rear 3.5in x12 + 3.5in x2 rear 3.5in x12 + 2.5in x4 rear 2.5in x24 NVMe no rear 3.5in x12 Hybrid with NVMe U.2 no rear The 24-bay front takes ONE rear, the 4 x 2.5 inch, which figure 19 numbers 24-27. The 12-bay front takes either, and figure 19 numbers both from 12. This device carries the 24-bay front, which is why its rear reads 24-27. THE ARITHMETIC GOT THERE FIRST AND IS NOW REDUNDANT. Bays numbered 12-15 imply eleven bays this model does not have; that is how the error was found. Table 28 is how it is now SOURCED, and a guess agreeing with a document afterwards is worth more than either alone. THE RISER SIDE IS TABLE 25, and its discriminator is riser 2 rather than riser 3. Rear storage is offered in riser configurations 0, 1 and 2 and no others: 1 and 2 fit a one-slot low-profile riser 2 (2B or 2C, slot 4 only), while configuration 3 fits a three-slot 2A (slots 4, 5, 6) and has NO rear storage despite fitting no riser 3 at all. It is riser 2's full-height section that occupies the bay the rear cage needs. This device's configurations already encode exactly that - rear storage only with rc0, rc1 and rc2 - and row 3 is `rc3-1a2a`, added when the riser 3 opening and rear storage bay 3 turned out to be the SAME HOLE, closed by two different blanks depending on which configuration you picked. RE-READ AND STILL OPEN: that change touched which bay closes an opening, not the front-to-rear coupling this gap is about. Re-read again when riser 1's brackets moved 1 mm and slot 2 lost its numeral on 1A - both are ink and geometry inside one bay, and neither reaches across faces. Re-read a third time when riser 1's plate grew to meet the slot strip and the shroud: the bay's own box moved, and still nothing crossed a face. A fourth time when riser 2's three slots were aligned and its plate cut back to the full-height pair. That one surfaced a NEW question but not a new gap of this kind: a bay's occupant is drawn after the panel, so a card cannot be shown "only through its cutout" without a part drawn after the bays to mask it. Recorded where it belongs, on the riser 2 slot 6 cutout, rather than widened into this one. A fifth time when the screw tab was split out of the frame so it could draw in front of riser 2's bracket tails. That is a draw-order fact about one bay, not a coupling between faces. A sixth time when riser 3 became bay 1 reflected - mirrored brackets, a two-slot plate and its own slot strip. Handedness is a fact about one bay's own metal and reaches no further than that. A seventh time when riser 3 slid 9.525 right to sit over the power supply's edge. Moving one bay along its own face changes nothing about which front it can be sold with. An eighth time when two "rivet" pairs beside the divider turned out to be card retention clips. A misread of what is on the rear, corrected on the rear, and silent about any front. A ninth time when those rivets came back, scoped: they are what the riser cage mounts to and they show when drives are fitted instead. That one is a rear configuration telling two rear drawings apart, which is the mechanism this gap says is MISSING between faces - and still is. A tenth time when the C20 supply became its own part. A second occupant for an existing bay, on the same face, coupled to nothing at the front. TWO SOURCES DISAGREE AND ARE LEFT DISAGREEING. The system information label draws FIVE fronts - 24, 16 and 8 x 2.5 inch, 12 and 8 x 3.5 inch - where table 28 lists TWO front backplanes. Whether the 16- and 8-bay fronts are different chassis or one backplane drawn part-populated, nothing held here says. AND TABLE 28 HAS A MID DRIVE TRAY in three of its ten rows. This device models no mid bay at all, which is a whole third drive location missing rather than a detail.
gaps.wanted: NOW DEMONSTRABLE RATHER THAN HYPOTHETICAL. `rear-2-lff` draws a correct 2 x 3.5 inch rear on a 24 x 2.5 inch front, and ISM table 28 lists no such machine - every row carrying that rear has a 12-bay front. The mismatch even forced an id: the figure prints 12 and 13, which are already two of this chassis's front bays, so the rear ones had to be rear-drive-12 and rear-drive-13. An id clash is what this gap looks like from the inside. RE-READ AFTER THE REAR BAYS WERE SEPARATED, and still open. The rear half of this is now expressible: the chassis structure across bays 2 and 3 is its own always-present part, and what each bay holds - drives, PCIe, a blank - varies independently of the other. That was the piece `only-in` could not reach while one 287 mm component owned both bays. WHAT REMAINS IS THE FRONT. The 24 x 2.5 inch and 12 x 3.5 inch fronts are different panels, not different occupancy, and until the second is drawn nothing exercises the face-binding that would couple it to a rear. A way for a configuration to constrain more than one view at once. Today `only-in` scopes a bay to a configuration and every view chooses independently, so nothing stops a consumer selecting a 24-bay front and a rear numbered 12-15 - a machine that cannot be bought. The library needs either configurations that span views, or a declared incompatibility between them; and this device needs its 12 x 3.5 inch front modelled before either can be exercised, which is the same gap `rear-2-lff` already stands on.

devices.description: 1RU 19-inch chassis for the DCP transponder and muxponder family. Two half-width traffic slots at the front; two hot-pluggable PSUs, a four-fan tray and the management board at the rear.

gaps.note: UM s3.1.5 says "The air inlets and outlets are positioned in the front and back", but fig 2-4 is an empty chassis shot into a dark cavity and resolves no vent pattern on the chassis front itself. The populated render (fig 1-1) does show honeycomb mesh, but that mesh is on the TRAFFIC UNITS' faceplates, not the chassis. So the front view draws no vent of its own and whether the chassis carries any is unresolved.
gaps.wanted: a face-on photograph of a populated DCP-2, which would show the chassis front beside a unit faceplate and separate the two. Every front image in the corpus is either an empty chassis or a three-quarter render.

gaps.note: These four views carry the ENVELOPE ONLY - the 440 x 45 x 500 box from the manual's spec table, with the front faceplate shown edge-on as a dark band - and no observed surface detail: no lid screws, no side rails, no ventilation. That is the same treatment dcp-r-9d-cs gives its four, and it is honest rather than complete. The populated three-quarter render (fig 1-1) does show the lid and the left flank, but it is a lit marketing render on a black ground at an angle that measures nothing.
gaps.wanted: a square-on photograph of the lid and of one flank. Failing that, the 3/4 render would support screw positions on the lid if it were rectified, which is what was done for smartoptics/dcp-404@1's top face.

gaps.note: The management board is called "mgmt-board" in the DCP-2-FB/HW ordering description and "part of the DCP-2 chassis" in UM s2.6, and it has no orderable part number of its own. Its ports are placed directly on the rear view with the plate drawn as decor, rather than modelled as a bay.
gaps.wanted: a statement either way on whether the board is field-replaceable. If it is, this becomes a bay accepting a management-board component, and the seven ports move onto that part.
